**What move is coming, and what can the offense do about it, this snap and the next?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The speed rush, around the corner: a dip and rip.** This is the rush plan paying off from the other direction. Twice
the rusher won inside, so the tackle has stopped bailing: he is sitting short and square to protect the inside. But a
tackle who has not gained depth has no time to get back to the corner, and the rusher meets him level before he can
turn and run. The spin is
the wrong answer now; that is exactly the move the tackle is sitting on.

The offense has fewer answers on this snap than you might think. The right guard cannot help outside, because the
3-technique is on him. The quarterback's best move is to step up into the pocket, so the rusher's arc carries him past
behind. **Next snaps:** the tackle varies his sets (a [jump set](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jump-set) at the line,
or a [45-degree set](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd) instead of sitting) so the rusher cannot read
the set and pick the counter; the offense chips the rusher with a back or tight end on the way out; and the play caller
calls quick throws, so the ball is gone before any move can finish. That is the conversation across a game in
miniature: the rusher made the tackle afraid of one thing, and now the offense has to change the question.
:::
:::

## Back to the replay

Return to the play that opened the chapter. Third-and-8, four rushers, an end who took three strides up the arc and
then drove straight into the tackle: **speed-to-power**, set up by every speed rush he had shown before. The tackle,
fearing the corner, had kicked back fast, so his weight was going backward when the end turned into him, and he could
not anchor. The pocket collapsed from the side, the quarterback threw early, and the pass sailed.

The box score has nothing for the end. FTN's charters would mark that dropback as pressured. Pass rush win rate might well
count it as a win, though a bull rush that never sheds the blocker is the kind of rep a beat-the-block measure can
miss. And a stopwatch would put the pressure at
about two seconds, early enough that it was entirely the rush's doing. That is the whole chapter in one snap: the
moves, the plan that set them up, and the reason a coach values the hurry that nobody counts more than the sack total
everybody does.

## Takeaways

- **The rush is a race and a fight.** A rusher must beat a bigger blocker before the ball is out, a little under three
  seconds on average. Get-off decides where they meet: a tenth of a second is most of a yard, and meeting the tackle
  level at the corner instead of in front of him is the difference between winning and losing.
- **Each move punishes a mistake.** Speed beats a slow set; the bull rush and long arm beat a high, light or retreating
  one; the swim, rip and spin beat a blocker who has committed. Cross-chops and ghosts beat the punch itself.
- **The best rushers have a plan.** They show one move until the tackle adjusts, then use the counter his adjustment
  opens; speed-to-power works *because* tackles fear speed.
- **Stunts win with geometry.** T-E, E-T and interior twists exchange rushers to beat man blocking or choose matchups
  against slides, at the cost of time and of lanes.
- **Four rush lanes make a box.** Ends keep contain, the middle pushes the pocket; against a quarterback who runs,
  the mush rush squeezes instead of racing and accepts a longer clock.
- **Count pressure, not sacks.** Pressure carries over from season to season and predicts future sacks; the share of
  pressures that become sacks mostly does not, except as a trait of the quarterback. Pass rush win rate, get-off and
  time to pressure use tracking data to take the quarterback out of the measure.

**Sets up:** [Blitzing](07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd), where the defense stops trying to win with four and adds
rushers instead, and [Zone Blitzes and Simulated Pressure](07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd), the modern art
of making four rushers come from places the protection did not expect; [Third Down](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd),
for spies and rushing three; and [Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd),
where you will measure get-off and time to pressure on real frames. The data section's metrics are mapped against the
rest of football's numbers in [Expected Points and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd).

**Case study:** [The Eagles: Trenches, RPOs and the Tush Push](../12-case-studies/12-06-eagles-trenches-and-tush-push.qmd),
including Super Bowl LIX's four-man pressure.
